title: Buffett 1982 letter: economic vs accounting earnings and why issuing undervalued stock destroys value
summary: Buffett explains why look-through "economic" earnings matter more than reported accounting earnings, why commodity-like industries (including insurance) earn poor returns without differentiation or a cost edge, and why issuing undervalued stock for acquisitions hands over $2 of value for $1. He also lists his acquisition criteria and the owner-like managers he prizes.

principles.text: Accounting earnings are the start, not the end, of valuing a business; count retained earnings of partly-owned companies regardless of ownership percentage.
principles.quote: managers and investors alike must understand that accounting numbers are the beginning, not the end, of business valuation.

principles.text: Buy businesses where each retained dollar eventually becomes at least a dollar of market value; the manic auction market gives the value investor an edge.
principles.quote: it is our job to select businesses with economic characteristics allowing each dollar of retained earnings to be translated eventually into at least a dollar of market value.

principles.text: Price paid matters enormously: overpaying for an excellent company can wipe out a decade of good results.
principles.quote: For the investor, a too-high purchase price for the stock of an excellent company can undo the effects of a subsequent decade of favorable business developments.

principles.text: Commodity businesses with overcapacity earn poor returns unless they have a wide, sustainable cost advantage.
principles.quote: For the great majority of companies selling “commodity”products, a depressing equation of business economics prevails: persistent over-capacity without administered prices (or costs) equals poor profitability.

principles.text: Only issue shares when you receive as much intrinsic business value as you give; size and activity are not progress.
principles.quote: we will not issue shares unless we receive as much intrinsic business value as we give.

principles.text: Managers should avoid the thrill of the chase in acquisitions, and judge dilution by intrinsic value, not near-term EPS.
principles.quote: For in many of these acquisitions, managerial intellect wilted in competition with managerial adrenaline
